lines.show: A storm has just torn through a city's power lines.
Three inspection drones must launch right now, and each has three possible routes.
Some routes are short. Some fight a headwind. And some cross the same stretch of sky as another drone.
The dispatcher wants two things at once: spend as little battery as possible, and keep the drones apart.
Those goals pull against each other, and every drone's choice changes the others.
Three drones give 27 possible plans. Twenty drones would give 95 trillion.
This is SkyLanes: conflict-aware drone routing, solved with QAOA in Qiskit.
Every drone-and-route pair gets one qubit: nine in total. A 1 means this drone flies this route.
The score adds each route's battery cost, plus a safety weight µ times every stretch of sky two drones share.
That shared-sky term couples pairs of qubits, the kind of interaction a quantum circuit handles natively.
And one rule must always hold: each drone flies exactly one route.
QAOA works in rounds: a scoring layer tilts the odds toward good plans, a mixing layer moves between plans, and a classical optimiser tunes the angles.
We built two versions. The first enforces the one-route rule with a fine.
The second builds the rule into the circuit: an XY mixer that only ever swaps a drone's route for another of its own.
Every answer is checked against an exact classical baseline: all 27 plans, cross-checked with Qiskit's exact solver.
You can explore all of it in our live dashboard.
The map shows the plan QAOA picked. Here it matches the exact best plan.
Lower the safety weight, and drones take cheaper routes but share airspace, shown in magenta. Raise it, and they spend battery to stay apart.
Switch to the penalty version, and the chance of a best plan falls to random guessing. Switch back, and it is several times better.
Sample 4,096 shots to see the spread of answers. Each is checked classically, so the best plan is always recovered.
Live mode re-optimises the same circuit in the browser, at any setting. Its simulator matches Qiskit to 5 parts in a billion.
Across all runs, the built-in-rule version hit a best plan in 32 to 52% of shots: 3 to 10 times better than guessing.
The penalty version never beat guessing.
Real hardware is harder. At 1% gate error, success falls to about 3%.
And because chip qubits only talk to neighbours, our routing circuit needs routing too: about 2.5 times more gates.
Is quantum faster here? No. A classical computer checks every plan in microseconds.
What SkyLanes shows is a correct, verified quantum method, the design choice that makes it work, and what stands between it and real fleets.
Code, results and the live dashboard are linked in our submission.
